extracted.intended_audience: artists, writers, and readers interested in aesthetics and the nature of art
extracted.subtask_description: A set of aesthetic and ethical principles about art, the artist's life, and the role of suffering drawn from Oscar Wilde's De Profundis; useful as evaluative criteria or creative‑writing guidance on truth, form, humility, and imagination. Emphasises how personal experience (especially sorrow) should be accepted and transmuted into artistic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sorrow as the supreme emotion and the ultimate test of great art
rubrics_metrics.description: “I now see that sorrow, being the supreme emotion of which man is capable, is at once the type and test of all great art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilde argues that sorrow gives art its deepest truth and reality; behind sorrow there is always reality whereas joy/laughter can mask coarse temperament. He cites music, a flower, a child, and other modes of existence as expressive examples, and claims that out of sorrow 'have the worlds been built.' Use sorrow (genuine emotional depth) as a criterion for artistic seriousness and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth in art = unity of inward and outward
rubrics_metrics.description: “Truth in art is the unity of a thing with itself: the outward rendered expressive of the inward: the soul made incarnate: the body instinct with spirit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether form and content are inseparable: does the external representation (language, image, form) make visible the inward state or essence? Wilde contrasts mere resemblance or echo with this deeper unity; aim for works where form reveals the inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic life is self-development
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work (and the artist) should show evolution and growth: art as an instrument for the artist's own moral and aesthetic development. Priority is given to self-realisation rather than conformity to external rules or fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility as essential artistic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: “Humility...the last thing left in me, and the best: the ultimate discovery... It is the one thing that has in it the elements of life, of a new life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humility arises from surrender and loss; it is not something to be assumed artificially. Wilde treats humility as a necessary condition for genuine artistic renewal: artists must accept and internalise their experiences (including failure and shame) to proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and transform all experience (including degradation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have got to make everything that has happened to me good for me... the plank bed, the loathsome food... the dreadful dress... the silence, the solitude, the shame--each and all of these things I have to transform into a spiritual experience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criterion for creative work: does the artist incorporate difficult or base experiences and transmute them into higher, expressive art? Avoid denial or forgetting of experience; use the material of one's life (even humiliation) as raw material for art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be entirely and absolutely oneself (authentic individuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am far more of an individualist than I ever was. Nothing seems to me of the smallest value except what one gets out of oneself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity is measured by the degree to which a work springs from the artist's unique vision rather than external sanctions, fashions, or imposed systems. Personal symbols and internally created forms are preferable to borrowed, external ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only inwardly created symbols are truly spiritual
rubrics_metrics.description: “Only that is spiritual which makes its own form... Its symbols must be of my own creating.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spirituality or profundity in art requires self-made symbols and forms. Avoid relying on received ritual or conventions; evaluate whether the work's symbols feel organically produced from the artist's inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative sympathy is the secret of creation
rubrics_metrics.description: “He realised... imaginative sympathy which in the sphere of Art is the sole secret of creation. He understood the leprosy of the leper, the darkness of the blind...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key criterion: the artist's capacity for empathetic imagination—entering and portraying the lives of others—determines the work's power. Assess how well the piece conveys understanding of otherness, suffering, and varied human conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being merely a spectator; engage as participant
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde contrasts Marius (an 'ideal spectator' merely contemplating) with the artist's need to be more than a passive observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that are only aesthetically pleasing from a distance (spectator art) are limited; stronger works arise from active engagement and lived experience. Evaluate whether the artist moves beyond detached contemplation to committed involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art is symbolic because man is symbolic
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art is a symbol, because man is a symbol.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work functions symbolically—whether elements stand for deeper human conditions and future development of the self. Good art reveals more than literal content; it points to broader human meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not deny or forget painful experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: “When first I was put into prison some people advised me to try and forget who I was. It was ruinous advice... To deny one's own experiences is to put a lie into the lips of one's own life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a writer's honesty: suppression of painful truth weakens art and stunts development. Works should acknowledge and integrate difficult truths of life rather than attempting to erase them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffering is not meaningless; it can yield humility and creative renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: “Now I find hidden somewhere away in my nature something that tells me that nothing in the whole world is meaningless, and suffering least of all. That something... is Humility.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or producing work, consider whether pain/suffering are rendered as generative and meaningful—leading to humility, insight, and new artistic possibility—rather than merely tragic or nihilistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: The artist should aim for unity where soul and body are indivisible
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde: the artist seeks 'the mode of existence in which soul and body are one and indivisible: in which the outward is expressive of the inward.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether characters, images, and form manifest an integrated being rather than fragmented surface/detail; aim for expressive coherence between interior states and external portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is limited; deeper art arises from embracing the whole garden (including shadow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde recounts living for pleasure but realising he had 'confined myself so exclusively to the trees of what seemed to me the sun-lit side of the garden, and shunned the other side for its shadow and its gloom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art that covers only pleasurable surfaces is incomplete. Evaluate whether a work explores both light and shadow—pleasure and pain—finding richness in contrast and totality of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: The artist's work should aim to rob malice of its venom by producing beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: “If I can produce only one beautiful work of art I shall be able to rob malice of its venom, and cowardice of its sneer, and to pluck out the tongue of scorn by the roots.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One practical standard: art's power to transform reputation and counteract scorn through beauty and excellence. Consider whether a work attains a level of excellence that compels re-evaluation or silences detractors.
